title: Sir Isaac Newton: Greatest Scientist of All Time?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck profile Isaac Newton as one of the most important contributors to modern science, covering his childhood and schooling, the 1665-66 "year of miracles," the scientific method, the Principia (three laws of motion and universal gravitation), Optics and the reflecting telescope, the calculus priority dispute with Leibniz, alchemy and religious beliefs (Arianism, biblical chronology), his later work at the Royal Mint, his knighthood, and his rivalries with Robert Hooke and John Flamsteed. The episode opens with tour announcements and a discussion of Newton's birthday under the Julian and Gregorian calendars, and ends with listener mail about fruitcake and craft beer hops.

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening
segments.summary: Hosts announce upcoming tour dates and ticket info, with a sponsor read for Squarespace, then open the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Newton
segments.summary: Hosts banter about pop culture and introduce Isaac Newton, citing Science World's claim that he is the most important contributor to modern science, and frame him as bringing order to 17th-century science.

segments.title: Newton's contributions, averaging data, and beliefs
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Newton's introduction of data averaging, his reliance on earlier thinkers, his religious belief in an orderly God, and his interest in ancient wisdom and alchemy-like pursuits, including his self-given name.

segments.title: Newton's birthday and calendar discrepancy
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Newton's birthday falls on different dates under the Julian and Gregorian calendars, and that Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar well after Catholic nations.

segments.title: Newton's birth and childhood
segments.summary: Newton was born prematurely in 1643 to a farming family; his father died before he was born, and he was raised largely by his maternal grandmother after his mother remarried. The hosts discuss the effects of this rejection on his personality.

segments.title: Posthumous diagnoses and mercury poisoning
segments.summary: The hosts discuss posthumous claims that Newton had Asperger's or autism, which they say are questionable, and the theory that mercury poisoning from alchemy contributed to his second nervous breakdown.

segments.title: Schooling at Cambridge
segments.summary: Newton was a weak student and poor farmer, went to Cambridge working as a servitor, self-educated beyond the syllabus, and was championed by Isaac Barrow, who helped secure him a scholarship.

segments.title: Year of miracles and the apple story
segments.summary: Newton returned home when plague closed Cambridge, and the hosts discuss the so-called year of miracles (annus mirabilis) and the apple-falling story, which they say is likely a fairy tale though Newton promoted it.

segments.title: Scientific method, Principia, laws of motion and gravity
segments.summary: The hosts describe how Newton refined the scientific method, and how the Principia introduced the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, building on Galileo's work.

segments.title: Optics, prisms, and the reflecting telescope
segments.summary: Newton showed white light is a spectrum of colors using a prism, delayed publishing Optics until 1704 due to dislike of criticism, and built a reflecting telescope that won him admission to the Royal Society.

segments.title: Calculus and the Leibniz dispute
segments.summary: Newton developed calculus, which he called the fluxions, and a dispute arose with Leibniz over who invented it; historians now think both developed it independently.

segments.title: Rivalries, alchemy, and religious views
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Newton's rivalry with Robert Hooke, his secret alchemy studies, belief in the Philosopher's Stone, biblical chronology predicting the end of the world, and his adherence to Arianism.

segments.title: Later life, Royal Mint, knighthood, and epitaph
segments.summary: Newton became Warden and later Master of the Royal Mint, where he moved the pound to a gold standard and pursued counterfeiters, was knighted in 1705, and was president of the Royal Society. The hosts also cover his treatment of John Flamsteed and his epitaph.

segments.title: Listener mail: fruitcake and craft beer hops
segments.summary: A listener defends fruitcake and the hosts discuss a Slate article complaining about hoppy beer, plus thanks to sponsors and listeners for gifts.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to contact and social media.
